item.title: Nvidia opens investigation after report CEO Jensen Huang was target of foreign intelligence
item.description:
Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, and his wife, Lori Huang, with Apple's Tim Cook at the top table during a state dinner hosted by Donald Trump for Xi Jinping at the White House in September. Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images

Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, and his wife, Lori Huang, with Apple's Tim Cook at the top table during a state dinner hosted by Donald Trump for Xi Jinping at the White House in September. Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images
Nvidia opens investigation after report CEO Jensen Huang was target of foreign intelligence
CEO reportedly ‌had close relationship ‌with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to ‌Beijing
Nvidia said ⁠on Sunday it “is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”.
The New York Times reported in ​October that Donald Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence that Huang ‌had a close relationship ‌with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to ‌Beijing.
Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump downplayed the revelations about Huang, who is an influential adviser to the president on artificial intelligence, saying: “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it.”
Trump also brushed off a question about whether he now regrets not acting on the intelligence when he was briefed on it, and suggested that he would be happy to take Huang with him on a trip to Asia next week. “I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong,” Trump said. “He dealt with somebody. But, you know, so does everybody else.”

item.title: The Guardian view on a tale of two activists: Joshua Wong and Au Kam San should not be behind bars | Editorial
item.description:
‘Joshua Wong was sentenced after pleading guilty to “foreign collusion”.’ Photograph: Fazry Ismail/EPA
View image in fullscreen
‘Joshua Wong was sentenced after pleading guilty to “foreign collusion”.’ Photograph: Fazry Ismail/EPA
The Guardian view on a tale of two activists: Joshua Wong and Au Kam San should not be behind bars Editorial
The latest vindictive prosecutions and harsh sentences in Hong Kong and Macau are further testimony to China’s ruthless suppression of dissent
One is internationally famous – he was once dubbed “the Face of Protest” by Time magazine – and the other is little known outside his home town. What Joshua Wong and Au Kam San share, beyond the harsh sentences they received last week, is that they represent the spirit of dissent that Beijing is determined to crush.
Mr Wong, who has been in prison for six years, should have walked free next January – not free to fight for Hong Kong’s rights, which China has suppressed so decisively, but at least to walk the streets of the city he loves. Instead, a court last Thursday sentenced the 30-year-old, an activist from the age of 14, to another 10 years. He is the only person to have been prosecuted twice under the draconian national security law (NSL). The case’s timing means that he will remain behind bars until he is 40 because so little of his sentences overlap. It also came one day after the city’s annual summit for global financial leaders ended – avoiding awkward questions for companies such as Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs, which long ago decided that it is business as usual, even as China turns the screw.
View image in fullscreen
Au Kam San. Photograph: Bertha Wang/AP
Mr Wong was sentenced after pleading guilty to “foreign collusion” – the same charge used against the newspaper tycoon Jimmy Lai, a British citizen, who was jailed for 20 years this spring. item.title: Chinese carmaker BYD’s offices in Netherlands raided over JLR ‘copycat car’ claim
item.description:
Land Rover’s new Defender, a successor to one of the most popular road vehicles. Photograph: Land Rover/PA
View image in fullscreen
Land Rover’s new Defender, a successor to one of the most popular road vehicles. Photograph: Land Rover/PA
Chinese carmaker BYD’s offices in Netherlands raided over JLR ‘copycat car’ claim
Bailiffs reportedly seized digital records before court case over alleged intellectual property breaches on Land Rover Defender
Bailiffs acting for Jaguar Land Rover raided the Dutch offices of a Chinese “copycat” rival before a legal showdown this week over whether its “Defender clone” infringes intellectual property rights.
Bailiffs acting on behalf of JLR reportedly seized digital records from the offices of Chinese carmaker BYD in Schiedam and Hoofddorp in August, according to the Sunday Times.
The raid took place before a court case in the The Hague this week which will decide whether the BYD has a case to answer over allegations that its Ti7 SUV infringes the intellectual property of the Land Rover Defender.
Motoring experts have likened BYD’s seven-seat plug-in hybrid SUV to the Defender since it went on sale in China in September last year. The company is scheduled to launch the vehicle, which the BBC’s Top Gear magazine called the “Chinese Defender clone”, in the UK market in January at a price of £47,995, undercutting the Defender by more than £20,000.
BYD says on its website that “an unapologetically boxy profile delivers the imposing, chunky design that finds favour among SUV buyers, yet delivers a contemporary look”.

item.title: Uyghurs facing deportation by Thailand say they will be ‘like slaves’ in China
item.description:
Two Uyghur men at risk of deportation from Thailand have shared letters with human rights groups saying they do not want to go back to China. Illustration: Guardian Pictures/EPA
View image in fullscreen
Two Uyghur men at risk of deportation from Thailand have shared letters with human rights groups saying they do not want to go back to China. Illustration: Guardian Pictures/EPA
Uyghurs facing deportation by Thailand say they will be ‘like slaves’ in China
Activists fear Bangkok will give in to pressure from Beijing despite reports of torture and human rights abuses against the mostly muslim ethnic minority
The deportation of two more Uyghurs to China from Thailand would put their lives in grave danger, activists have said, with one of the men saying he would be “like a slave” if he was sent back.
Last year, Thai authorities forcibly deported 40 Uyghur men to China despite pleas from the men themselves and the UN.
The US and Canada had reportedly offered to resettle them, but Bangkok appeared to want to avoid upsetting Beijing. The UN has said the returnees’ whereabouts remain unknown.
Now, two more men fear becoming the latest victims of Beijing’s repressive crackdown against the largely Muslim ethnic group, condemned by the UN as a potential crime against humanity.
The girlfriend of one of the men said her boyfriend, whose name is being withheld for security reasons, told the Guardian he wanted to go “anywhere else but China”.
Human rights groups said two Uyghur men were at risk of deportation after recently being transferred to an immigration detention centre and they feared Thai authorities may once again give in to pressure from Beijing.
Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch, called for the men to be allowed to travel to a safe third country. “Previous Thai governments have kept Uyghurs in inhumane detention for years and then complied with Beijing’s demands to send them to China, where they were forcibly disappeared,” she said.

item.description:

View image in fullscreen
Traditional Russian wooden dolls depicting China's President Xi Jinping, the US president, Donald Trump, and Russia’s Vladimir Putin. The three leaders could meet in China later this month. Photograph: Dmitri Lovetsky/APExplainer
Ukraine war briefing: Beijing confirms historic Xi-Trump-Putin meeting under discussion
Russia could use tri leader summit to nudge China and US closer to its position on Ukraine, experts say. What we know on day 1,718
Beijing has confirmed that it is discussing a historic meeting between Chinese leader Xi Jinping, the US president, Donald Trump, and Russia’s Vladimir Putin. Mao Ning, a spokesperson for the Chinese foreign ministry, said at a press briefing this week in Beijing that China “is in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state”, which could take place on the sidelines of the Apec summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen this month.
Russia would probably use the summit to nudge China and the US closer to Moscow’s positions on Ukraine, said Sun Yun, director of the China program at the Stimson Center. However, Trump has been warned by his advisers to steer clear of Ukraine as a topic of the discussions, said Danny Russel, a former senior state department official who served in Barack Obama’s administration and who is now a distinguished fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
Ukraine again came under attack from Russia on Saturday, after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy repeated his calls for allies to supply Kyiv quickly with missiles for the US-made Patriot system to defend Ukrainian cities. item.title: EU charges TikTok with failing to protect users’ mental health
item.description:
The Chinese-owned short-video platform, which has 189 million users in the EU, was found to have failed to prevent users from being served up repetitive content on themes such as body image or isolation. Photograph: Josef Kubes/Alamy
View image in fullscreen
The Chinese-owned short-video platform, which has 189 million users in the EU, was found to have failed to prevent users from being served up repetitive content on themes such as body image or isolation. Photograph: Josef Kubes/Alamy
EU charges TikTok with failing to protect users’ mental health
Regulator’s initial ruling says algorithm ‘can be harmful’ and led young and vulnerable viewers ‘down rabbit holes they can’t easily escape’
TikTok has been charged by the European Commission with failing to protect users’ mental health by exposing them to a relentless stream of content that risks worsening eating disorders and anxiety in a case that strikes at its business model.
Issuing a preliminary ruling on Friday, the EU regulator said TikTok’s algorithm “can be harmful” and was leading young and vulnerable users “down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from”.
The Chinese-owned short-video platform, which has 189 million users in the EU, was found to have failed to prevent users from being served up repetitive content on themes such as body image or isolation, which can lead to anxiety, sadness, worsen existing eating disorders or mental health problems.
Officials said their investigation focused on legal content, where a single video might not be problematic, but the cumulative effect of watching scores of them on one theme could damage users’ mental health.
TikTok’s safeguards to mitigate the risks of “rabbit-hole effects” – where users are served narrow and repetitive content to keep them engaged – were found to be ineffective. item.title: In jailing Joshua Wong, China is telling the world they'd crush every hope for democracy on its soil | Nathan Law
item.description:
Joshua Wong delivers a speech outside the offices of Hong Kong's chief executive Leung Chun-ying in Hong Kong, 3 October 2014. Photograph: Tyrone Siu/Reuters
View image in fullscreen
Joshua Wong delivers a speech outside the offices of Hong Kong's chief executive Leung Chun-ying in Hong Kong, 3 October 2014. Photograph: Tyrone Siu/Reuters
In jailing Joshua Wong, China is telling the world it would crush every hope for democracy on its soil Nathan Law
My friend was due to be released next January. Under draconian security laws, his sentence has been extended by 10 years
Two years ago, I wrote in this newspaper about the lengthy imprisonment of my friend Joshua Wong, who I spent years campaigning alongside for the advancement of Hong Kong’s democracy. He was given an unjust sentence meant to keep him behind bars until January 2027. He was supposed to be released in a few months, when I hoped he would finally be able to reunite with his friends and family and embark on a new chapter.
But this hope was misplaced. The end of the tunnel isn’t next year; it’s late 2036. By then, he will be 40. On Thursday, Joshua was sentenced to another 10 years under Hong Kong’s national security law for colluding with foreign forces. He is the only political prisoner who’s been convicted twice under the national security law. The judge described Joshua and me as “two ringleaders or masterminds” urging foreign powers to impose sanctions and other hostile actions against the Chinese and Hong Kong governments. The judgment cited previous international advocacy work, media interviews, social media posts and the political activities of Demosistō, the youth-led democratic party we founded.
Much of the cited evidence predates the implementation of the national security law, even though the court insisted it was not being applied retrospectively. item.title: UK and US condemn ‘cruel’ second jail term handed to Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong
item.description:
Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong, pictured in 2019, is the only person to have been prosecuted twice under the legislation that critics say has been used to silence political opposition in the city. Photograph: Jérôme Favre/EPA
View image in fullscreen
Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong, pictured in 2019, is the only person to have been prosecuted twice under the legislation that critics say has been used to silence political opposition in the city. Photograph: Jérôme Favre/EPA
UK and US condemn ‘cruel’ second jail term handed to Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong
Foreign Office says 10-year sentence shows city’s security law is being used to ‘target individuals for political expression’
Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in prison in national security case
The UK and the US have condemned the 10-year sentence given to Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong under a controversial national security law.
Wong, 30, was sentenced on Thursday after pleading guilty to “foreign collusion” under the law. He is the only person to have been prosecuted twice under the legislation that critics say has been used to silence political opposition in the city.
A spokesperson for the UK Foreign Office said that Wong’s sentence was “a clear example of how the National Security Law is being used to target individuals for political expression and participation”.
The spokesperson added: “We call for an immediate end to all unjust prosecutions of individuals charged under the National Security Law and urge the authorities in China and Hong Kong to honour the rights and freedoms guaranteed to the people of Hong Kong under the Sino-British joint declaration (1984).”

item.title: Raise the Red Lantern review – Gong Li gives a decade-defining performance in an addictively ruthless masterpiece
item.description:
Unforgettable … Gong Li in Raise the Red Lantern. Photograph: Era International/Kobal/Shutterstock
View image in fullscreen
Unforgettable … Gong Li in Raise the Red Lantern. Photograph: Era International/Kobal/ShutterstockReview
Raise the Red Lantern review – Gong Li gives a decade-defining performance in an addictively ruthless masterpiece
Gong simmers with rage, loneliness and humiliation as the ‘fourth mistress’ navigating the intimate political savagery of her husband’s compound in Zhang Yimou’s 1991 drama
Revisiting Zhang Yimou’s grippingly addictive psychological drama from 1991, adapted from a novella by Su Tong, is a reminder of what a great impact this movie made on western audiences. They responded to its arguably westernised tale of a young woman’s desperate loneliness in a sinister environment that resembles something by Charlotte Brontë or Daphne du Maurier. Like Jung Chang’s memoir Wild Swans from the same year, Raise the Red Lantern opened our eyes to 20th-century China’s secret theatre of cruelty and misogyny; elaborate domestic rituals of submission and servitude coexisted with infinitely subtle plotting, resentful manoeuvring and covert denunciation, habits of thought that could so easily be absorbed into Maoism.
Gong Li gives one of the great performances of the 1990s as Songlian, a beautiful, intelligent young woman in 1920s China who is forced to abandon her university studies after just six months because her father has died and there is no longer money for the fees. In the unforgettable opening scene, which unfolds with a single unbroken shot of Gong’s pale face, incandescent with shock and pain, Songlian announces to her callous stepmother (who remains off camera) that she is ready to accept marriage – and then her eyes brim with tears. Her suppressed rage, loneliness and humiliation are to simmer below the surface for the rest of the film.

item.title: Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in prison in national security case
item.description:
Joshua Wong in 2019. He gained international attention during the 2014 Umbrella protests. Photograph: Kin Cheung/AP
View image in fullscreen
Joshua Wong in 2019. He gained international attention during the 2014 Umbrella protests. Photograph: Kin Cheung/AP
Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in prison in national security case
Wong, 30, in prison since 2020, is only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under national security law
Exclusive: Joshua Wong laments city’s fate from inside maximum security prison
The Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong has been sentenced to 10 years in prison after earlier pleading guilty to “foreign collusion”, his second conviction under a national security law critics say has been used to silence political opposition in the city.
Wong, who rose to prominence as the teenage face of Hong Kong’s 2014 pro-democracy demonstrations, submitted his guilty plea in September. He had been accused of working with the exiled Hong Kong activist Nathan Law to urge foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades or other hostile measures against China.
In his ruling on Thursday, the high ​court judge William Tam ‌described Wong’s actions as “grave in nature”.
He said Wong had visited the US to seek foreign interference before the national security law’s introduction in 2020, and continued to share posts on social media by Law calling for sanctions after it was enacted.
Wong’s role was to “supply his underground support” and “arouse the attention of foreign countries to bolster the cause”, the judge said. He described Wong’s actions as part of a “scheme” to collude with foreign governments.
View image in fullscreen
A prison van believed to be carrying Joshua Wong arriving at the high court in Hong Kong on Thursday. Photograph: Vernon Yuen/Nexpher/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock
Tam said Wong’s sentence would run concurrently with the remaining term of his previous national security offence.

item.description:
Delivering net zero also at risk, say MPs as they call for centralised policy and funding for mines and diversification

The UK is “dangerously” dependent on China for critical raw materials needed for the military, renewable energy infrastructure and AI, a parliamentary investigation has found.

MPs on the business select committee called for an urgent centralised policy and the creation of a “critical minerals finance facility” to help fund rare earth and other critical mineral mines, and deploy grants, equity and debt to accelerate a diversification programme.

item.title: Choke of the century? Chengdu collapse sets up thrilling Chinese Super League climax
item.description:
John Aloisi’s players need a point on the final day to seal their maiden title – but their form has dropped off a cliff

With four games of the Chinese Super League to go, Chengdu Rongcheng needed just a point to clinch their first title. With one game to go, they still need a point. What was a formality has become a formidable task. The biggest bottle job in Asian football history is very much on and it would be as popular as it would be dramatic.

The coach of the Sichuan club, the former Portsmouth and Coventry striker John Aloisi, has seen a 12-point lead over Dalian Yingbo cut to just three before Sunday’s showdowns. Whatever happens, this is a positive and thrilling end to a season that started negatively – literally – with nine of the 16 top-tier clubs kicking off on minus points.
